s: Bound angle with the knees moving up and down. Warms the hips before any deeper opening.
Butterfly Flaps approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
Ankle crossed over the opposite knee while seated. The figure-four hip opener for chairs and desks.
One leg lifted over the shoulder and extended straight while the torso rotates. Among the most demanding seated shapes for hamstring and shoulder range together.
Compass Pose taken with a block under the supporting hand or beneath the seat. The prop shortens the distance to the floor so the spine can stay long instead of rounding to reach it.
in: Compass Pose with Block (Parivrtta Surya Yantrasana (block))

s: Knees stacked and arms clasped behind the back in opposite directions. Simultaneously one of the hardest hip and shoulder openers.
Cow Face Pose taken with a block under the supporting hand or beneath the seat. The prop shortens the distance to the floor so the spine can stay long instead of rounding to reach it.
Cow Face Pose approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
One shin cradled in the arms and rocked side to side. Opens the outer hip without loading the knee the way pigeon can.
Cradle Stretch taken with a block under the supporting hand or beneath the seat. The prop shortens the distance to the floor so the spine can stay long instead of rounding to reach it.
Cradle Stretch approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
Walking forward in a deep squat. Classically prescribed for digestion and among the most heating of the simple practices.
Shins crossed and stacked with the torso folding forward. A gentler entry to the firelog shape for tighter hips.
Double Pigeon taken with a block under the supporting hand or beneath the seat. The prop shortens the distance to the floor so the spine can stay long instead of rounding to reach it.
Double Pigeon approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
Three-legged dog with the hip opening and the knee bending. Opens the outer hip but stresses the sacroiliac joint if the shoulders collapse.
in: Downward Dog Split Twist (Eka Pada Adho Mukha (open hip))

s: Downward Dog Split Twist approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
in: Downward Dog Split Twist with Strap (Eka Pada Adho Mukha (open hip) (strap))

s: The yin form of a deep lunge held for several minutes. Targets connective tissue rather than muscle.
Shins stacked one directly above the other. One of the most intense external hip rotations available seated, and unforgiving of knee compensation.
Firelog Pose taken with a block under the supporting hand or beneath the seat. The prop shortens the distance to the floor so the spine can stay long instead of rounding to reach it.
Firelog Pose approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
Knees wide and shins out with the hips sinking toward the floor. A very strong adductor opener that must be entered slowly.
Frog Pose taken with a block under the supporting hand or beneath the seat. The prop shortens the distance to the floor so the spine can stay long instead of rounding to reach it.
Frog Pose approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
The frog shape with the feet against a wall so the depth can be controlled precisely.
A deep squat with heels down and elbows pressing the knees wide. The everyday resting squat of much of the world, and a strong hip opener for those who have lost it.
Garland Pose taken with a block under the supporting hand or beneath the seat. The prop shortens the distance to the floor so the spine can stay long instead of rounding to reach it.
Garland Pose approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
Front shin angled across the mat, back leg extending straight behind. The most widely taught hip opener in modern classes.
Half Pigeon taken with a block under the supporting hand or beneath the seat. The prop shortens the distance to the floor so the spine can stay long instead of rounding to reach it.
in: Half Pigeon with Block (Eka Pada Rajakapotasana (prep) (block))

s: On the back with knees drawn wide toward the armpits and feet held. Opens the hips while the low back stays flat and safe.
Happy Baby approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
A deep lunge with both hands inside the front foot and forearms often lowering. Opens the hip in flexion and the groin at once.
Lizard Pose taken with a block under the supporting hand or beneath the seat. The prop shortens the distance to the floor so the spine can stay long instead of rounding to reach it.
Lizard Pose approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
Back knee down, hips sinking forward, arms often overhead. The primary hip flexor opener and a staple of the sun salutation cycle.

Low Lunge approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
Rocking between a low lunge and a half split. Works hip flexors and hamstrings alternately.
in: Lunge to Half Split Flow (Anjaneyasana-Ardha Hanumanasana)

s: A supported wide squat used through pregnancy to open the pelvis. Held with support rather than depth.
Supine hand-to-toe with the leg opening out to the side. Adductor length without any balance demand.
in: Reclined Big Toe Side (Supta Padangusthasana II)

s: Cow face legs taken lying down. Removes the spinal load while keeping the hip opening.
Ankle crossed over the opposite thigh with the legs drawn in. The figure-four shape, and the accessible version of pigeon for stiff or injured hips.
Reclined Pigeon approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.

s: A lunge with both hands framing the front foot and the back leg long. The most common transitional shape in vinyasa.
Runner's Lunge approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
The yin version of cow face legs, held long. One of the most effective outer hip releases available.
A wide lateral lunge with the torso upright. The gentler precursor to skandasana.
Side Lunge approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
Side-lying leg raises. Simple conditioning for the outer hip and lateral trunk.
Lying on one side and catching the top foot behind. A safe quadriceps stretch with no balance demand.
A deep side lunge with one leg straight and the other bent to a squat. Opens the adductors under load.
Skandasana approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
The yin form of pigeon, held long and unforced with the torso folding down.
Side-lying with the top leg lifted and held at the toe. Named for Vishnu reclining on the cosmic serpent.
Firelog held in the yin manner for several minutes. Intense and slow rather than muscular.
A wide-footed squat with the torso upright, less demanding on ankle range than malasana and better tolerated by stiff hips.
Standing Wide Squat taken with a block under the supporting hand or beneath the seat. The prop shortens the distance to the floor so the spine can stay long instead of rounding to reach it.
in: Standing Wide Squat with Block (Prasarita Malasana (block))

s: Standing Wide Squat approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
in: Standing Wide Squat with Strap (Prasarita Malasana (strap))

s: Seated with one leg lifted over the shoulder and extended while the torso opens.
The supine figure-four with the hands drawing the underneath thigh toward the chest.
The deep squat held for several minutes rather than seconds. Restores a range most adults have lost.
Headstand with the forearms crossed rather than the fingers interlaced.
Shoulderstand with a belt around the upper arms to hold the shoulder position. An Iyengar solution to collapsing elbows.
Shoulderstand fully supported on a chair with the shoulders on a bolster. The Iyengar restorative inversion.
Handstand facing the wall so the body must find true vertical rather than banana back.
Downward dog on the forearms. The single best preparation for forearm stand and a strong shoulder builder in its own right.

Dolphin Pose practised with the wall as a reference. The wall removes the fear of falling and lets the alignment be felt rather than guessed, which is how the shape should be learned before it is held alone.
in: Dolphin Pose at the Wall (Ardha Pincha Mayurasana (wall))

s: Dolphin with alternating leg lifts against a wall. The safe drill for building forearm stand.

Dolphin to Forearm Stand Drill practised with the wall as a reference. The wall removes the fear of falling and lets the alignment be felt rather than guessed, which is how the shape should be learned before it is held alone.
in: Dolphin to Forearm Stand Drill at the Wall (Pincha (prep) (wall))

s: Pedalling the heels in downward dog to release each calf in turn.
in: Downward Dog Calf Stretch (Adho Mukha (calf pedal))

s: Hands on a wall at hip height with the torso horizontal. Teaches the shoulder action of downward dog without the weight.
in: Downward Dog at Wall (Adho Mukha Svanasana (wall))

s: Downward dog with hands elevated on blocks. Reduces the wrist angle for anyone with wrist pain.
An inverted V with hips lifting and heels descending. The most-used shape in modern practice and a mild inversion in its own right.
Plough with the knees folding beside the ears. Deeper spinal flexion still, and only appropriate once plough is entirely comfortable.

Ear Pressure Pose practised with the wall as a reference. The wall removes the fear of falling and lets the alignment be felt rather than guessed, which is how the shape should be learned before it is held alone.
in: Ear Pressure Pose at the Wall (Karnapidasana (wall))

s: From shoulderstand, the lotus legs folding down toward the chest. A deeply compressed closing shape.
Forearm stand entered with the hands clasped. More stable at the base and harder to press up into.
A full inversion balanced on the forearms. Demands more shoulder flexion than handstand and is often easier to hold once entered.

Forearm Stand practised with the wall as a reference. The wall removes the fear of falling and lets the alignment be felt rather than guessed, which is how the shape should be learned before it is held alone.
in: Forearm Stand at the Wall (Pincha Mayurasana (wall))

s: From shoulderstand, the feet lowering to the floor behind the head. Very strong on the cervical spine and never to be entered by dropping.

Halasana Plough practised with the wall as a reference. The wall removes the fear of falling and lets the alignment be felt rather than guessed, which is how the shape should be learned before it is held alone.
A full inversion on the hands. The most athletically demanding shape in the catalogue and the one that most rewards patient wall work.
Small hops toward vertical from a downward dog base. The safe way to find the balance point before committing to the full inversion.

Handstand Hops practised with the wall as a reference. The wall removes the fear of falling and lets the alignment be felt rather than guessed, which is how the shape should be learned before it is held alone.
in: Handstand Hops at the Wall (Adho Mukha Vrksasana (prep) (wall))

s: Handstand with the spine arching into a scorpion shape. Among the most advanced postures practised.
Balanced on the forearms and crown with the body vertical. The king of asanas classically, and the shape with the highest injury cost when learned without supervision.
Headstand with the legs moving into splits, wide angle or lotus. Only appropriate once the base is unshakeable.
Downward dog with the hips supported in wall ropes so the spine can traction. Distinctly Iyengar.
in: Iyengar Wall Rope Dog (Adho Mukha Svanasana (rope))

s: Headstand with the legs folding into lotus. Requires both a solid headstand and a comfortable lotus.
Shoulderstand with the legs in lotus and the knees pressing into the hands.
Headstand with the arms free and palms flat, offering far less base than the bound version.
Dolphin Pose with one leg lifted. Halving the base doubles the demand on the supporting side and exposes any left-to-right imbalance immediately.
in: One-Legged Dolphin Pose (Eka Pada Ardha Pincha Mayurasana)

s: Ear Pressure Pose with one leg lifted. Halving the base doubles the demand on the supporting side and exposes any left-to-right imbalance immediately.
in: One-Legged Ear Pressure Pose (Eka Pada Karnapidasana)

s: Forearm Stand with one leg lifted. Halving the base doubles the demand on the supporting side and exposes any left-to-right imbalance immediately.
in: One-Legged Forearm Stand (Eka Pada Pincha Mayurasana)

s: Halasana Plough with one leg lifted. Halving the base doubles the demand on the supporting side and exposes any left-to-right imbalance immediately.
Handstand with one leg lifted. Halving the base doubles the demand on the supporting side and exposes any left-to-right imbalance immediately.
in: One-Legged Handstand (Eka Pada Adho Mukha Vrksasana)

s: Handstand Hops with one leg lifted. Halving the base doubles the demand on the supporting side and exposes any left-to-right imbalance immediately.
in: One-Legged Handstand Hops (Eka Pada Adho Mukha Vrksasana (prep))

s: Shoulderstand with one leg lifted. Halving the base doubles the demand on the supporting side and exposes any left-to-right imbalance immediately.
Three-Legged Dog with one leg lifted. Halving the base doubles the demand on the supporting side and exposes any left-to-right imbalance immediately.
in: One-Legged Three-Legged Dog (Eka Pada Eka Pada Adho Mukha Svanasana)

s: Tripod Headstand with one leg lifted. Halving the base doubles the demand on the supporting side and exposes any left-to-right imbalance immediately.
in: One-Legged Tripod Headstand (Eka Pada Sirsasana II)

s: Moving between plough and shoulderstand with control rather than momentum.
The closing shoulderstand of the Ashtanga sequence, held long before plough and ear pressure.
Forearm stand with the spine arching and the feet reaching toward the head. Inversion and deep backbend at once.
Body vertical on the shoulders with the neck supported. Called the queen of asanas in the classical literature, and genuinely risky for the cervical spine when unsupported.
Shoulderstand with the legs moving into splits, wide angle or lotus.
Shoulderstand with the feet against a wall to control the load on the neck. How the pose should be learned.

Shoulderstand practised with the wall as a reference. The wall removes the fear of falling and lets the alignment be felt rather than guessed, which is how the shape should be learned before it is held alone.
The yin form of plough with a rounded spine held long. Considerable load on the cervical spine and not for beginners.
Headstand practised with the wall behind so the legs cannot swing past vertical. The honest way to learn the shape.
Shoulderstand with folded blankets under the shoulders so the cervical curve is preserved. The Iyengar standard, and the only version many teachers will now teach.
Plough with the legs wide and the big toes gripped, then rolling up to a seated fold.
Downward dog with one leg lifting behind. The standard preparation for stepping through to a lunge.
in: Three-Legged Dog (Eka Pada Adho Mukha Svanasana)

s: Three-Legged Dog practised with the wall as a reference. The wall removes the fear of falling and lets the alignment be felt rather than guessed, which is how the shape should be learned before it is held alone.
in: Three-Legged Dog at the Wall (Eka Pada Adho Mukha Svanasana (wall))

s: A headstand with the hands forward forming a tripod. The entry point for many arm balance transitions.

Tripod Headstand practised with the wall as a reference. The wall removes the fear of falling and lets the alignment be felt rather than guessed, which is how the shape should be learned before it is held alone.
in: Tripod Headstand at the Wall (Sirsasana II (wall))

s: Scorpion entered from handstand rather than forearm stand, with straight arms throughout.
Handstand held with the heels resting on a wall. Where the strength and alignment are actually built.
A supported shoulderstand variant with the legs floating rather than fully vertical.
Alternate nostril breathing extended with counted ratios and retention. The bridge between simple breathing and formal pranayama.
Kapalabhati performed kneeling, the closing practice of the Bikram sequence.
Steady unblinking gaze at a candle flame until the eyes water, then holding the afterimage. A concentration practice classed among the cleansing kriyas.
Kneeling with arms overhead, pulling the navel in rhythm with a chanted mantra. The central Kundalini kriya.
Rapid forceful exhalations with passive inhalations. Classically a cleansing kriya rather than a pranayama, and strongly heating.
Isolating and rolling the abdominal recti on an empty breath. The most difficult kriya to learn and among the most strongly claimed for digestion.
A cross-legged seat with one heel at the perineum, named for the adepts. Favoured in the hatha texts over lotus for long pranayama sessions.
A shortened rotation of consciousness through the body. Suitable at the end of any practice in place of a longer savasana.
Full lotus with the arms crossing behind to catch the opposite toes.
Holding attention on a single object. The sixth limb, and the discipline that makes dhyana possible.
A simple cross-legged seat with the spine upright. The default meditation posture when lotus is unavailable, which for most adults it is.
One foot drawn onto the opposite thigh, the other tucked beneath. The usual stepping stone toward full lotus and a stable seat in its own right.
Both feet drawn onto the opposite thighs. The classical seat of the texts, and one that must come from external hip rotation rather than knee torque.
Silent or whispered repetition of a mantra, often counted on a mala. The most widely practised meditation technique in the tradition.
Sustained undirected awareness in a stable seat. The seventh limb, and the destination the physical practice is arranged to serve.
Meditation seated in a chair with the feet flat and spine free of the backrest. The stable seat for most modern practitioners.
Deliberately withdrawing attention from sensory input. The fifth limb and the hinge between the outer and inner practices.
Slow deliberate walking with attention on each footfall. The classical alternative when sitting is not possible.
A guided rotation of awareness through the body while lying completely still. Deeply restorative and the most accessible entry to formal meditation.
Breathing through one nostril at a time in a fixed cycle. The most widely prescribed balancing pranayama and the safest to self-practise.
Forceful inhalation and exhalation in equal measure. The most heating breath practice in the repertoire and not for beginners.
A rapid even-paced diaphragmatic breath from the Kundalini tradition, distinct from kapalabhati in rhythm.
Inhaling through a rolled tongue. Explicitly cooling, and the classical answer to excess pitta or summer heat.
Arms at sixty degrees with breath of fire, from the Kundalini repertoire. Strongly heating and named for its intent.
Inhale and exhale matched to the same count. The simplest way to steady an agitated breath and the entry to all ratio work.
Lengthening the exhale to roughly twice the inhale. The most direct breath lever on the parasympathetic system.
Inhaling through clenched teeth with a hiss. The alternative to sitali for those who cannot roll the tongue.
A soft humming on every exhale with the ears closed. Reliably calming and one of the few practices with reasonable modern evidence for anxiety.
Ujjayi practised seated and still rather than during movement. Where the quality of the breath can actually be examined.
The opening breath of the Bikram series, standing with fingers interlaced under the chin.
Filling the belly, then the ribs, then the upper chest in one long inhale. The first breath practice taught and the foundation for the rest.
A soft constriction at the glottis giving the breath an audible ocean quality. The default breath of vinyasa practice.
Ujjayi with deliberate breath retention after inhale or exhale. Retention is where pranayama becomes genuinely risky without a teacher.
in: Victorious Breath with Retention (Ujjayi with Kumbhaka)

s: Eight points touching the floor — knees, chest and chin — as the gentler alternative to chaturanga in classical sun salutations.
Face-down rest with the arms extended forward. Prescribed traditionally for a strained low back.
Lying on the back curved into a crescent. A long passive stretch of the whole side body and the intercostals.
The banana curve held long on each side, targeting the fascial line from armpit to hip.
A supported bridge with blocks under both the sacrum and the shoulders.
in: Block Between Blocks Bridge (Setu Bandha (two blocks))

s: Kneeling and folding forward with the forehead down. The universal resting shape and the one to return to whenever a practice becomes too much.
Lying with knees bent and feet planted so the low back can release. The alternative to savasana for anyone whose back complains lying flat.
Lying completely still on the back. The hardest asana to do properly and the one the whole practice is arranged to make possible.
Final rest with a bolster under the knees and support under the head. The version most low backs actually need.
Puppy pose supported on blocks so the heart opening can be held for minutes. Named for the heart centre it is said to work on.
Final rest guided by voice through progressive release. The bridge between savasana and yoga nidra.
Reclining lengthways over a bolster so the thoracic spine opens passively. A modern restorative staple.
Prone rest with the hands clasped behind the neck and the elbows down.
Legs up the wall with a bolster raising the pelvis. Deepens the mild inversion while remaining entirely passive.
in: Legs Up Wall with Bolster (Viparita Karani (bolster))

s: Lying with the legs vertical against a wall. A mild inversion with most of the benefit and almost none of the risk of shoulderstand.
Lying with the calves resting on a chair seat. The gentlest way to unload the lumbar spine.
Lying prone with the forehead on stacked forearms. The classical prone rest between backbends.
The flapping fish pose, prone with one knee drawn up to the side. Traditionally recommended for sleep and digestion.
Hips high, chest and chin melting toward the floor. A yin shape held for minutes rather than breaths.
A kneeling surrender pose with the forehead down and arms extended forward, held in stillness.
Left-side-lying rest with support between the knees. The recommended final rest after the first trimester.
Final rest taken face down. Often more settling than the supine version for an anxious nervous system.
Forearms on a chair seat with the chest melting down. A shoulder opener that needs no floor work.
Bound angle taken lying down, usually over a bolster. One of the most reliably calming shapes in the whole restorative repertoire.
Reclined bound angle with blocks under the thighs so the groin can release without strain.
in: Reclined Butterfly with Blocks (Supta Baddha Konasana (blocks))

s: A supine twist with the knees resting on a bolster so nothing has to be held. Suitable for long holds and for pregnancy.
Final rest taken on the side with support between the knees. The recommended form in pregnancy and for anyone uncomfortable on the back.
Reclined bound angle with a strap holding the legs so no muscular effort is needed. The standard long-hold restorative hip shape.
in: Supine Bound Angle with Strap (Supta Baddha Konasana (strap))

s: A long passive backbend over a bolster or backbender. Opens the thoracic spine without any effort.
Bridge with a block under the sacrum so the shape is held without effort. A passive chest opener and a mild inversion.
Child's pose over a bolster so the torso is fully carried. Suitable for very long holds and for pregnancy with the knees wide.
Fish taken over a bolster so the chest opens without any muscular effort. One of the best shapes for a desk-bound upper back.
A seated fold resting the torso entirely on a bolster. Quiet and long rather than deep.
Half frog supported on a bolster so the quadriceps releases without a knee demand.
A long passive twist with the knees resting on a bolster to one side.
Legs wide against a wall while lying on the back, gravity doing the work over several minutes.
Child's pose with the knees wide so the belly can settle between the thighs. Better tolerated in pregnancy and by larger bodies.
Rotating the ankles in both directions. The first movement in the classical pawanmuktasana joint series.
Ankle Rotations approached with a strap. The strap stands in for a reach the shoulders or hamstrings cannot yet make, so the shape is entered honestly rather than forced into a rounded compromise.
Kneeling with the tops of the feet flat and the knees lifted. The counterpose to the toe squat.
